The paper was published in 1959 in IEEE Transactions on Antennas and Propagation.
Saxon's method reformulates wave propagation problems as exact integral equations using Green's functions.
The WKB approximation emerges as the zeroth-order approximation of Saxon's formulation.
The method is applicable to both isotropic stratified media and scattering by isolated inhomogeneities.
For total reflection problems, the local wave number K²(z) is assumed linear near the turning point: K²(z) ≈ (z₀ - z)2N₂₀.
The Green's function is constructed using Bessel functions C₁ and C₂ that are exact solutions of the linear turning point problem.
The correction to WKB results depends on the function X(z), which vanishes identically where K²(z) is strictly linear.
The phase shift δ in total reflection represents a change in the apparent location of the reflecting layer.
For scattering problems, the method handles both scalar and vector electromagnetic fields.
The mixing integral in vector problems is responsible for annihilating longitudinal components of scattered radiation.
Polarization corrections for a dielectric sphere are of order (ε-1)² compared to primary scattered field of order (ε-1).
The method reduces to Langer's approach whenever a physical problem involves an ordinary differential equation with a turning point.
Convergence of the iterative solution is rapid when spatial variations of the local index of refraction are gradual.
The method provides explicit expressions for corrections to the WKB result through the correction integral.
For large angle scattering (KR₀²>>1), the method yields specific expressions for the scattering amplitude.
The slowly varying condition requires that the change in refractive index over a wavelength be very small compared to the refractive index.
The method was sponsored in part by Republic Aviation Corporation and Farrington Daniels Laboratory.
Saxon's approach generalizes the method of Fermat and the geometrical optical approximation.
The method is applicable to problems involving total reflection by the ionosphere.
Straight line ray paths with WKB phase are used in practical calculations rather than full optical ray paths.
The method enables calculation of both close-in electric fields and scattering amplitudes.
Polarization effects are examined explicitly in the scattering formulation.
The method has been applied to study propagation in nonisotropic stratified media for both transmission and total reflection cases.
The integral equation formulation is exact, though practical calculations require iterative or other appropriate techniques.
The method provides a precise mathematical basis for assumptions commonly made in traditional WKB treatments.
